title: Automation is spreading faster than intervention plans
mainJudgement: Automation is spreading faster than intervention plans.

committeeQuestion.question: For one important automated workflow, who can stop or change it—and can management show that authority works?
committeeQuestion.why: As systems move from assisting people to taking action, the practical control is not a policy. It is a named person, a real permission boundary and a route that works under pressure.
committeeQuestion.evidence: The workflow, its permissions, the named intervention authority, the stop or rollback route and one recent test or decision record.

committeeQuestions.question: Which important customer services would fail together if a shared cloud, identity, data or model provider were impaired—and when did we last test the fallback?
committeeQuestions.why: Individual supplier assessments can miss a common dependency. A disruption becomes the firm’s problem when multiple important services depend on the same underlying provider or control plane.
committeeQuestions.evidence: The service-and-dependency map, common points of failure, impact tolerance, fallback plan, test result and accountable owner.

committeeQuestions.question: Can management trace one recent cyber or data issue from alert to closure, including the decision, action, exception and proof that the fix worked?
committeeQuestions.why: Seeing an alert is not the same as controlling the risk. The committee needs confidence that an issue can be identified, owned, remedied and closed with evidence that survives scrutiny.
committeeQuestions.evidence: The original alert, named owner, decision log, remediation record, any accepted exception, retest result and dated closure record.

judgement.observation: AI is moving from helping people to carrying out work. NIST is exploring a faster, more automated approach to vulnerability management, while a Bank of England paper keeps cloud concentration firmly in the banking risk frame.
judgement.executiveJudgement: The risk is not simply more technology. Automation, asset data and critical-service dependencies often sit in different teams. When a service fails or an automated process behaves badly, it can be unclear who may intervene, change access or invoke a fallback.
judgement.implication: Choose one automated workflow and one important cloud service. Test the permission boundary, the data and suppliers it depends on, the fallback plan and the person who can intervene. If those answers are not clear, expansion is moving faster than control.
